Your Drone Is Missing
Add-ons for the drone you already own: an indoor hover with no GPS, a
sensor ring that refuses to hit a wall, a parachute that saves it when it
falls, a gimbal, a landing pad it finds by itself, and a payload that maps
the invisible. Every one bolts onto a standard flight controller.

drone upgrades — a Build List field guide
1 / 16

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand optical flow (velocity from image motion), why flow must be scaled by height, how a flight controller’s
estimator fuses a new sensor, and how to configure and validate that fusion safely. That is the core of GPS-denied
navigation.
→the job this maps to: drone autonomy and GNC engineering — indoor-drone, inspection, and navigation teams.

!
PROPS OFF FIRST
Configure and verify every new sensor with the propellers removed, watching the data in your ground station. Make
the first hover low, in a large clear room, with a hand on the sticks and nobody else inside — and never over people.
That rule applies to every upgrade in this guide.
// how it works
UPGRADE 01 · REV A
Optical flow: The sensor sees floor texture move across its tiny image and reports pixel displacement per frame — the
angular rate of the ground beneath. It is a mouse sensor pointed at the floor from a metre up.
Height turns flow into velocity: The same angular rate means a faster ground speed when you are higher, so the flight
controller needs the height from a rangefinder (a ToF like the VL53L1X or a TFmini) to scale flow into linear velocity.

Fusion in the estimator: The flight controller’s EKF fuses flow velocity with the IMU and the rangefinder into a position
estimate whose drift is bounded by the flow — no GPS required. It also enables terrain-following altitude hold.
▸

Light and texture: Flow needs texture and light: a blank floor or a dim room starves it. A small downward LED and a
textured surface make the difference between a locked hover and a drift.
▸
Flight modes: With flow enabled, position-hold and loiter modes work indoors, and the controller arbitrates between GPS
and flow depending on what is healthy. Understanding that arbitration is what keeps a hybrid indoor / outdoor flight safe.

[ U P G R A D E 0 1 ]
Indoor Position Hold
Rock-steady hover in a room with no GPS — a $12 sensor that watches the floor

$35
beginner
1 weekend
// why this matters
Outdoors, GPS tells the flight controller where the drone is. Indoors there is no GPS, and a drone drifts like a balloon in a draft.

The fix is the same trick an optical mouse uses: a tiny downward camera (a PMW3901 optical-flow sensor) watches the floor
texture slide by and reports velocity, while a rangefinder gives height. Feed both to the flight controller and it holds position —
a hover you can let go of, indoors, that stays put. It is the cheapest, most dramatic upgrade there is, and it is the foundation
for every kind of indoor autonomy.

Mount the sensors
Fix the flow sensor and rangefinder facing straight down, clear of props and landing gear. Alignment matters: a tilted
flow sensor reads motion that isn’t there.
Wire and enable
Connect flow (SPI or UART) and rangefinder (I2C or UART) to the flight controller, enable both in parameters, and
confirm live readings in the ground station — props off.
Calibrate the flow scale

Move the drone by hand over a textured floor and compare flow-reported motion to the IMU; adjust the flow scale
parameters until they agree.
Verify the estimator

With props still off, check that the EKF reports a healthy flow-based position estimate. Only then fit props.
4
Hover and let go

In a clear, well-lit room, take off low in position-hold and slowly release the sticks. Watch it stay put. Then test terrain-
following over a step and note where flow breaks (dark floor, low texture).

drone upgrades — a Build List field guide
3 / 16

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand multi-sensor proximity sensing, sector-based obstacle representation, streaming sensor data to a

flight controller over a standard protocol, and how avoidance behaviour (stop versus slide, safety margins) is designed
and tuned. That is core drone-safety and autonomy engineering.
→the job this maps to: drone safety and autonomy engineering — inspection-drone, delivery, and consumer-drone
perception teams.

!
A SAFETY LAYER, NOT A PILOT
Avoidance has blind spots (between sensors, above, below) and hard limits (glass, bright sun, speed). Test it slowly,
low, in a clear space with a spotter, and never treat it as permission to fly near people. It catches mistakes; it does not
replace the pilot.

UPGRADE 02 · REV A
[ U P G R A D E 0 2 ]
Obstacle-Avoidance Sensor Ring
A ring of ToF sensors that stops your drone before it hits the wall — and slides it away

$50
intermediate
1–2 weekends
// why this matters
A drone that can feel the walls is a fundamentally safer drone. Mount a ring of time-of-flight distance sensors around the

frame, have a small microcontroller stream the nearest obstacle in each direction to the flight controller as proximity data,
and the controller’s own avoidance logic takes over: fly toward a wall and the drone stops short, or slides along it, no matter
what the sticks say. Push it toward a doorway and it refuses to hit the frame. It is the flagship of this guide — sensing,

integration, and control behaviour in one upgrade — and it is the same layered safety architecture real autonomous drones
use.

drone upgrades — a Build List field guide
4 / 16
// how it works

BUILD NOTE
Six VL53L1X modules at 60° spacing is the cheap version; four TFmini-S give longer range. Either way, the

microcontroller sends standard MAVLink OBSTACLE_DISTANCE messages, so the flight controller’s built-in avoidance
does the hard part — you don’t write the control loop.
// key design decisions
// bill of materials

COMPONENT
PART / SPEC
QTY
~COST

ToF sensors (×6)
VL53L1X (or 4× TFmini-S)
6
$36

Microcontroller
ESP32 / Arduino as sensor bridge
1
$8

Ring mount
printed ring / brackets
1
$5

Wiring
cables, connectors
—
$2
Sectors, not a single beam: One ultrasonic sensor sees one direction. A ring of ToF sensors reports the nearest obstacle
in each sector around the drone, giving the controller a 360° picture of the horizontal clearance.
Speaking the controller’s language: A microcontroller reads every sensor and packs the distances into a standard

proximity message over the telemetry port. The flight controller ingests it exactly as it would a commercial sensor — it just
works.
Stop or slide: With avoidance enabled, the controller applies a margin: approach an obstacle and it either halts the drone
at the margin or lets it slide along the obstacle. Both are tunable, and the choice changes how the drone feels to fly.
Field of view and gaps: Each sensor covers a cone; between cones there are gaps, and nothing covers above or below.
Sensor count, spacing, and mounting angle set how complete the picture is.
What ToF can’t see: Glass, mirrors, very dark surfaces, and bright sunlight fool infrared ToF. Speed matters too — at high
speed the drone can outrun its own reaction distance. Knowing the limits is part of the design.

Why a ring of ToF sensors instead of one ultrasonic sensor? A single sensor sees one narrow direction and ultrasonics
are slow and wide-beamed. A ring of fast, narrow ToF sensors gives clearance in every horizontal direction, updated many
times a second — the minimum for the drone to react to a wall it is drifting toward, not just one it is facing.

Why send proximity to the flight controller instead of overriding the sticks yourself? The flight controller already has the
state estimate, the motor mixing, and a tested avoidance algorithm with proper margins. Feeding it standard proximity

data means your sensors plug into that safety logic instead of fighting it with a home-made override that could destabilise
the aircraft.
Why is this not autonomy? Avoidance is a reflex: it prevents contact within its field of view at modest speeds. It has gaps,

it can be fooled, and it plans nothing. Real autonomy adds mapping, planning, and redundancy on top. Treating avoidance
as a safety net rather than a self-flying feature is the honest engineering position.

5 / 16
// build steps
// interview questions
Build the ring

Mount six ToF sensors at 60° spacing on a printed ring around the frame, facing outward and level, clear of props. Wire
them to the microcontroller.
Read every sector
Program the microcontroller to poll all sensors and print the six distances. Wave a hand around the drone and confirm
each sector responds.
Stream to the flight controller
Send the distances as MAVLink OBSTACLE_DISTANCE messages over a telemetry port. Confirm the ground station’s
proximity view shows your sectors live — props off.
Enable avoidance and set margins
Turn on the controller’s avoidance, set a conservative margin (a metre or more) and choose stop or slide. Hover in a
clear space and slowly push toward a wall: it should stop short.
Tune and map the limits

Adjust margins and behaviour, test corners and doorways, then deliberately find the failure modes — glass, sun, speed
— and document them. Knowing where it fails is the deliverable.

drone upgrades — a Build List field guide
6 / 16

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand freefall detection from an IMU, failsafe logic and false-trigger rejection, mechanical deployer design,
canopy sizing from descent-rate physics, and the test discipline (bench, drop, tethered, live) that a safety system
demands. Safety-critical design is a skill every aviation employer looks for.
→the job this maps to: drone safety-systems and aviation-safety engineering — delivery-drone, UAS-operations, and
airworthiness teams.

!
TEST IT LIKE IT MATTERS
A deployer is a spring or a gas charge under tension: keep hands clear of the tube, test with props off, and never stand

under a drop test. Use spring or servo release — no pyrotechnics. Do live deploy tests only over an empty field, well
within your local rules, and remember a canopy in the props is worse than no canopy: motor cut-off on deploy is
mandatory.
// how it works
UPGRADE 03 · REV A
Detecting the fall: In freefall the accelerometer reads near zero g on all axes. Detect that condition for longer than a set
time (a few hundred milliseconds, to reject bumps) and you have a reliable trigger. A failsafe signal from the flight
controller, or a manual channel, are the other triggers.
Cut the motors: On deploy, the props must stop instantly, or the canopy and lines wrap into them. The trigger sends a
motor-kill to the flight controller (or cuts ESC power) before the pin releases.
The deployer: A tube holds the packed canopy on a compressed spring, retained by a pin a servo pulls. Release the pin
and the spring throws the canopy clear of the airframe; a bridle and swivel connect it to the frame’s centre.

Sizing the canopy: Descent rate depends on canopy area and total mass; aim for roughly four to five metres per second.
Too small and the landing is a crash; too large and the pack won’t fit. The maths is simple drag physics.
▸

Testing a safety system: Bench trigger tests, then drop tests with a dummy mass from height, then tethered deploy, then
a live test over an empty field. A parachute you haven’t drop-tested is decoration.
▸

[ U P G R A D E 0 3 ]
Parachute Recovery System
A failsafe that senses freefall and pops a canopy — saves the drone, and whoever is
below it

$50
intermediate
1 weekend
// why this matters
Motors fail, batteries fail, and a drone that loses power becomes a falling brick. A parachute recovery system detects the fall

— or takes a command — kills the motors, and deploys a canopy so the aircraft comes down at a walking pace instead of
terminal velocity. Commercial systems cost hundreds; you can build one with a spring-loaded tube, a servo pin, an

accelerometer, and a properly sized canopy. It is the one upgrade that protects people on the ground as much as the drone, it
is increasingly what regulators want for flights near people, and the deployment shot is spectacular.

Size the canopy
Weigh your drone, choose a target descent rate, and compute the canopy area. Buy or sew a canopy to match and
pack it with a spring-loaded deployer tube.
Build the deployer
Print the tube, fit the spring and a servo-pulled retaining pin, and mount it at the frame’s centre with a bridle and
swivel. Confirm a clean, fast throw on the bench — props off.
Write the trigger

Detect near-zero g for a few hundred milliseconds on the IMU, plus a manual trigger channel. Wire a motor-kill to the
flight controller that fires before the pin releases.
Drop-test with a dummy

Drop the deployer with a dummy mass from height over soft ground, many times. Measure the descent rate and the
deploy delay; tune spring, packing, and trigger time.
Tethered, then live
Fit it to the drone, verify motor kill on trigger with props off, then do a tethered deploy and finally a live test over an
empty field at safe altitude. Film the deploy — and log the descent rate.

drone upgrades — a Build List field guide
8 / 16

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand gimbal mechanics and balancing, IMU-based attitude sensing on a moving base, field-oriented control
of brushless motors for smooth torque, PID tuning of a stabilisation loop, and vibration isolation. Stabilisation
engineering shows up across cameras, drones, weapons-sights, and satellites.
→the job this maps to: stabilisation and mechatronics engineering — camera-gimbal, drone-payload, and precision-pointing
teams.
// how it works

BUILD NOTE
Don’t write gimbal firmware from scratch. A STorM32 or SimpleBGC-class controller with its IMU handles FOC and

stabilisation; your engineering is the frame, the balance, the motor choice, the tuning, and the vibration mounting.
Balance first — an unbalanced gimbal can never be tuned smooth.
UPGRADE 04 · REV A

Sensing the camera’s attitude: An IMU mounted on the camera plate reports its pitch and roll at high rate. The
controller’s job is to hold that attitude at the target regardless of what the frame beneath it does.
▸

Gimbal motors and FOC: Gimbal brushless motors are high-pole-count, low-speed motors driven with field-oriented
control for smooth, cogging-free torque at zero speed — exactly what holding a camera still requires.
▸
The stabilisation loop: A PID loop per axis takes the attitude error and commands motor torque to cancel it. Tuning sets
the stiffness and damping: too soft and it wobbles, too stiff and it oscillates.
Balance is everything: If the camera’s centre of mass sits off the motor axes, the motors fight gravity constantly, wasting
torque and ruining smoothness. Mechanical balance on each axis before any tuning is the golden rule.
Isolating vibration: Motor and prop vibration reaches the gimbal through the frame; rubber dampers between drone and
gimbal filter it so the IMU sees camera motion, not airframe buzz.

[ U P G R A D E 0 4 ]
2-Axis Brushless Camera Gimbal
Buttery footage from a shaky drone — FOC gimbal motors that cancel every wobble

$60
advanced
1–2 weekends
// why this matters
Raw drone footage is a jittery mess because the camera rides every twitch of the airframe. A brushless gimbal fixes that: an

IMU on the camera measures its attitude hundreds of times a second and two brushless motors, driven smoothly with field-
oriented control, hold it level no matter what the drone does. Build one and your footage goes from home video to broadcast-
smooth. It is mechatronics, control, and the same FOC drive technology behind robot joints — and it is the upgrade that most
changes what your drone produces.

drone upgrades — a Build List field guide
10 / 16

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand fiducial detection and pose estimation, camera calibration, sending a landing target to a flight
controller over a standard protocol, the controller’s precision-landing behaviour, and failure handling when the target
is lost. That is the vision-to-control pipeline autonomous drones are built on.
→the job this maps to: drone autonomy and computer-vision engineering — docking, delivery, and autonomous-inspection
teams.

!
CLEAR PAD, EMPTY FIELD
Test precision landings over an empty field with a clear area around the pad and an abort ready on the sticks. Start

from low altitude and increase as it proves reliable. A drone descending onto a target is committed — make sure
nothing can be under it.
// how it works
UPGRADE 05 · REV A

Fiducials: An AprilTag or ArUco marker is a black-and-white pattern designed for reliable detection; from its corners in the
image, the software recovers the tag’s position and orientation relative to the camera.
▸
The companion computer: A small computer (a Raspberry Pi) runs the camera and the tag detector, then sends the
target’s offset to the flight controller as a standard landing-target message over the telemetry link.
The controller lands on it: In precision-landing mode, the flight controller uses the target offset to steer the descent,
correcting horizontally as it comes down so the drone stays centred over the pad.
Calibration and alignment: Camera calibration turns pixels into angles correctly; camera-to-body alignment turns those
into offsets the controller can act on. Get either wrong and it lands confidently next to the pad.

Losing the target: Tags disappear when the drone is too high, too tilted, or too close. Robust behaviour handles that: keep
the last estimate briefly, then fall back to a normal landing or abort.
▸

[ U P G R A D E 0 5 ]
Vision Precision Landing
It lands itself on a coaster-sized pad — a downward camera, an AprilTag, and a
companion computer

$55
advanced
2 weekends
// why this matters
GPS puts a drone down within a couple of metres, which is useless for docking, charging, or landing on a vehicle. Precision

landing uses a downward camera to see a fiducial marker on the pad, computes exactly where the pad is relative to the drone,
and steers the descent so it touches down centred — the technology behind every autonomous docking and charging drone.

Add a small companion computer, a camera, and a printed tag, and your drone lands itself on a pad the size of a coaster. It is
computer vision, coordinate transforms, and controller integration, and the demo is undeniable.

drone upgrades — a Build List field guide
12 / 16

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand payload integration (mass, power, isolation from the drone’s own RF noise), geotagged data logging,
survey flight planning, spatial interpolation into a heatmap, and interpreting RF propagation. Aerial survey and sensing
payloads are a growing engineering field.
→the job this maps to: drone-payload and aerial-survey engineering — inspection, mapping, and RF-survey teams.

!
RECEIVE-ONLY, YOUR OWN AIRSPACE
The payload only listens — it transmits nothing beyond your drone’s normal control link. Fly the survey within your
local rules: line of sight, altitude limits, not over people or others’ property, and keep the added mass well inside your
drone’s limits.

UPGRADE 06 · REV A
[ U P G R A D E 0 6 ]
Signal-Mapping Payload
Fly a grid and come back with a 3D heatmap of every radio signal in the air — a receive-
only survey payload

$50
advanced
1–2 weekends
// why this matters
A drone is the perfect platform for measuring things you can’t see from the ground — and radio is the best example. Strap on a

receive-only payload (an SDR or a WiFi scanner) with a GPS logger, fly a lawnmower grid at a few altitudes, and you come back
with a three-dimensional heatmap of signal strength: where your WiFi dies, how far your mesh radios reach, where

interference lives. It is the drone as a scientific instrument, it is receive-only, and it produces the one thing nobody else on
your feed has: a picture of the invisible over your own neighbourhood.

drone upgrades — a Build List field guide
13 / 16
// how it works

BUILD NOTE
Start with an ESP32 WiFi scanner (cheapest, lightest, logs every access point’s strength) before an SDR. Isolate the
payload’s antenna from the drone’s own transmitter, and always check hover time with the payload aboard — extra

mass shortens flights faster than you expect. Swap in a small thermal sensor and the same pipeline maps roof heat
loss.

The payload: A lightweight receiver (WiFi scanner or SDR), a GPS logger, and a battery, mounted away from the drone’s
own antenna so its transmitter doesn’t swamp the measurement.
Geotagged logging: Every measurement is stamped with position, altitude, and time, so each reading is a point in 3D
space. Logging rate sets your spatial resolution.
The survey pattern: A planned lawnmower grid at constant altitude covers the area evenly; repeating it at two or three
altitudes builds the third dimension. Mission planning makes it repeatable.

Reading the map: Signal strength varies with distance, obstacles, multipath, and your payload antenna’s own pattern.
Interpreting the map honestly — separating real coverage from artefacts — is the engineering.
▸

drone upgrades — a Build List field guide
15 / 16

WRAP · 6 UPGRADES FITTED
[ W R A P ]
Your drone is a platform —
the upgrades are the engineering.
An indoor hover, a wall it refuses to hit, a parachute, a gimbal, a pad it lands on by itself, a map of the invisible — six add-ons

that turn a stock quad into a sensing, self-protecting, self-landing instrument. The airframe is commodity; the value is in what
you bolt on and integrate: sensor fusion, avoidance logic, safety systems, stabilisation, vision, and payloads. That is exactly
the work drone and autonomy companies hire for, and it is far more impressive than a kit build.
// the skill ladder
Fit them in order and each one hands you the technique the next one needs:
sensing →avoidance →safety systems →stabilisation →vision autonomy →payloads

!
BEFORE YOU FLY
Know your local rules — registration, line of sight, altitude limits, no flying over people or near airports, lights at night —
and follow them. Bench-test every upgrade with the props off and verify the data before a single flight. Check mass

and centre of gravity after each add-on, keep failsafes configured, respect LiPo safety, and test new behaviours low,
slow, in an empty field, with a spotter. A drone is an aircraft; treat every upgrade like an airworthiness change.

DO THIS
Fit even one. Film it — a hover you let go of, a drone stopping short of a wall, a canopy popping mid-air, footage going
from shaky to glass-smooth, a touchdown centred on a coaster, a heatmap of your street — and put the config, code,
